one_liner: Header-only generalized Ziggurat sampler for gamma, Student t, F, Weibull and custom unimodal densities; 2.5-10x faster than STL distributions.
what_it_does: Zest samples from unimodal (including unbounded-at-mode) and monotone densities with the generalized Ziggurat algorithm of arXiv 1810.04744. The built-in distributions are normal, exponential, Laplace, Cauchy, semicircle, triangular, chi-squared (compile-time dof), gamma, Weibull, log-normal, Student's t and Fisher's F, and users can plug in their own pdf and strip_area class. The API is a class template Ziggurat<Distribution, URBG, N = 1024, float_type = double>: you construct it once (passing a distribution object when it has parameters) and call it as zig(urbg), like a std:: distribution but with the URBG type fixed at compile time.
how_it_is_fast: It uses Marsaglia-Tsang's Ziggurat idea, generalized: the constructor precomputes N equal-area horizontal strips (by bisection on strip_area), so most draws are one URBG call, a table lookup by the low index bits and one compare, with no log, exp or special-function evaluation. Only draws that land in a strip edge, the tail (mapping or mapping-plus-rejection) or an unbounded peak take the slow path. The README's largest ratios (6-20x) are for Student's t and Fisher's F, where this fast path skips all per-draw transcendental work.
when_to_use: Hot loops drawing millions of variates from a fixed-parameter Student's t, Fisher's F, gamma or Weibull distribution, where the README reports 2.5-10x over libstdc++ and 3.3-20x over Boost.
Exact sampling from your own unimodal or monotone density, including ones unbounded at the mode or with infinite tails, without hand-writing a Ziggurat: supply pdf, strip_area and a tail category.
GPL-compatible C++14+ projects that already depend on Boost (zest.hpp includes Boost.Math headers).
Monte Carlo code paired with a 64-bit URBG (std::mt19937_64 or any generator whose range is exactly 2^64) when you want full double resolution.
when_not_to_use: Proprietary or permissively licensed code: it is GPL-3.0, so vendoring the header puts your program under the GPL.

Parameters that change on every draw (for example a per-sample gamma shape in Dirichlet or Gibbs samplers): each parameter set needs a new Ziggurat object whose constructor runs N (default 1024) root searches, using Boost special functions for gamma/t/F, and the setup cost is not documented.
Normal or exponential only: per the README it only ties Boost for normal and log-normal (1.0) and is slower than Boost for exponential (0.67), so Boost or a small dedicated Ziggurat is simpler.
Multimodal densities, which the algorithm does not support.

Bulk or SIMD generation, or when you need tests and maintenance: it is a scalar, one-variate-at-a-time sampler with no test suite, CI or benchmark code in the repo, and it has been inactive since 2020.

integration.dependencies: Boost.Math headers (boost/math/special_functions/gamma.hpp, boost/math/distributions.hpp); ships with canonical_float_random.hpp alongside zest.hpp
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (enforced by #error), but the header uses message-less static_assert, a C++17 feature, so expect warnings in C++14 mode (errors with -pedantic-errors)
integration.platforms: any platform with a C++14 compiler and Boost; no SIMD or OS-specific code in the headers
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. operator() is const and only reads tables built in the constructor, so one object shared across threads with a separate URBG per thread looks safe from the code.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — call syntax matches a std:: distribution (zig(urbg)), but the URBG type is a template parameter, its range must be exactly 2^32 or 2^64 (std::minstd_rand fails a static_assert), and there is no param_type, reset(), min() or max(); output sequences differ from std::

gotchas: With a 32-bit URBG (the README example uses std::mt19937), each fast-path variate comes from one 32-bit draw whose low 10 bits pick the region, so body values carry only about 22 random bits (from reading operator()). Use a 64-bit URBG when double resolution matters.

Each object is large: with N=1024, double and a 64-bit URBG, the symmetric implementation holds four (N+1)-entry double tables, an N-entry int64 table and a 4096-double table, about 72 KB (derived from the class layout). Asymmetric distributions hold two monotone sides. Avoid putting many of them on the stack.

The constructor throws std::logic_error on bad parameters or very low rejection efficiency, and it prints WARNING lines to std::cerr for low-efficiency regions. zest.hpp uses std::cerr without including <iostream> and relies on Boost's includes.
Ziggurat is declared in the global namespace (only the distributions are in zest::), and ChiSquared takes its degrees of freedom as a compile-time template argument.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Zest over normaldist-benchmark, cxx-ziggurat or zigg when you need Ziggurat speed for non-normal shapes (t, F, gamma, Weibull) or a custom unimodal pdf. Those siblings cover only the normal (plus exponential and uniform in zigg). For vectorized bulk normal or uniform fills, EigenRand or Randompack fit better.
verified_claims_summary: The README gives 'approximate' relative speeds of Zest with 1024 regions vs STL / Boost: normal 3.6 / 1.0, exponential 3.3 / 0.67, gamma alpha>1 2.5 / 7, Student's t nu>1 10 / 20, Fisher's F d1,d2>1 6 / 11-14. No CPU, compiler, flags, URBG or benchmark code is given, and a search snippet of the arXiv preprint says the STL was GCC's libstdc++.
status_note: Abandoned since 2020-01-25 (6 commits; its one issue, an Exponential example crash, was fixed then). It is a self-contained header pair, but GPL-3.0 limits it to GPL-compatible projects.
